hero.title: The SOLID Principles
task.1.title: S - Single Responsibility: one animal, one job
task.1.context:
This is the **S** in SOLID: Single Responsibility. A class should have one job, so it has one reason to change.

Why bother - isn't this overengineering? When one class takes on two unrelated tasks, a change to one quietly risks the other. Here `Cat` both checks if it is hungry and builds the sign text the keeper reads. Reword the sign and you are editing the very method that decides feeding - one careless change breaks both. Keep them apart and a sign change can never touch the hunger check.

The fix: leave `Cat` with only the check, and move the sign text into its own `FeedingSign` class.
task.1.goal.0: Give `Cat` a `bool` field for its hunger, set in a constructor - so `IsHungry()` answers from the cat's own state, not a hardcoded `true`.
task.1.goal.1: Write a `FeedingSign` with `string Format(bool hungry)` returning `"FEED"` or `"FULL"`.
task.1.goal.2: `Main` builds a hungry cat, asks it, then formats the sign. The output stays `FEED`.
task.2.title: O - Open/Closed: add an animal without editing
task.2.context:
This is the **O** in SOLID: Open/Closed. Code should be open to new behaviour but closed to edits - you add a case without reopening what already works.

Why bother - isn't this overengineering? Every time you edit a working method to bolt on a case, you risk the cases that already passed, and you have to retest all of them. Here `AnimalVoice.Speak` grows another `if` for every animal. Add a cow and you reopen the same method cats and dogs already depend on. If each animal is its own class behind `IAnimal`, a new animal is a new class and the old ones are never touched - so they cannot break.

The fix: give each animal its own class behind a shared `IAnimal` interface.
task.2.goal.1: Write a `Cat` (`"Meow"`) and a `Dog` (`"Woof"`), each implementing `IAnimal`.
task.2.goal.2: `Main` uses a `Cat` through an `IAnimal` variable. The output stays `Meow`.
task.3.title: L - Liskov Substitution: the penguin that can't fly
task.3.context:
This is the **L** in SOLID: Liskov Substitution. Any subtype must be usable anywhere its parent is, with no surprises.

Why bother - isn't this overengineering? Inheritance looks like free reuse, but if the child cannot keep the parent's promise it becomes a landmine. A `Penguin` that inherits `Bird` still has a `Fly()` - so it throws, and any code holding a `Bird` crashes the moment it meets a penguin. The bug stays hidden until the wrong animal shows up. This starter throws when you run it.

The fix: drop the false is-a. Have both types share a small `IMover` and return a real move for every case, so none of them throws.
task.3.goal.1: Make `Sparrow` implement it (`Move` returns `"Fly"`) and `Penguin` implement it (`Move` returns `"Swim"` - never throw).
task.3.goal.2: `Main` moves a `Penguin` through an `IMover`. The output should be `Swim`.
task.4.title: I - Interface Segregation: don't make a fish walk
task.4.context:
This is the **I** in SOLID: Interface Segregation. A class should only depend on the methods it actually uses.

Why bother - isn't this overengineering? A fat interface forces a class to implement things it will never do, and those fake bodies are traps - other code can call them and blow up. Here one `IAnimalActions` demands `Walk`, `Swim` and `Fly`, so a `Fish` has to fake walking and flying with methods that throw. Split the interface and the fish implements only swimming - there is nothing fake left to call by mistake.

The fix: split the fat interface into small focused ones - `IWalker`, `ISwimmer`, `IFlyer` - so the fish implements only the one it needs.
task.4.goal.0: Declare three small interfaces: `IWalker` with `string Walk()`, `ISwimmer` with `string Swim()`, and `IFlyer` with `string Fly()`.
task.4.goal.2: `Main` uses the fish through an `ISwimmer`. The output stays `swim`.
task.5.title: D - Dependency Inversion: hand the keeper a log
task.5.context:
This is the **D** in SOLID: Dependency Inversion. High-level code should depend on an interface, not reach out and build a concrete class itself.

Why bother - isn't this overengineering? When a class creates its own dependencies, it is welded to those exact choices. Here `Keeper` builds its own `ConsoleLog` inside itself, so it can only ever log to the console - and in a test you cannot check what it logged without it printing for real. Have the keeper receive the log from outside and a test can hand it a fake that just records the message. That single move is what makes the class testable at all.

The fix: have `Keeper` receive an `ILog` through its constructor instead of building one. A test can then pass a fake log that records the message - the payoff you will lean on for testing.
task.5.goal.0: Declare `interface ILog` with `void Write(string message)`, and make `ConsoleLog` implement it.
task.5.goal.1: Change `Keeper` to receive an `ILog` through its constructor and store it in a `private readonly` field - no `new` inside.
task.5.goal.2: `Main` hands in a `ConsoleLog`. The output stays `cat fed`.
task.6.title: What you learned
task.6.context: The five habits in one place - what each one fixes.
task.6.summaryIntro: None of these are rules for their own sake. Each one saves you a headache the day the code has to change:
task.6.summaryItems.0.title: S - Single Responsibility -
task.6.summaryItems.0.text: One class, one job. While the hunger check and the sign text shared a method, a change to one could break the other. Give each its own class and a change stays where you put it.
task.6.summaryItems.1.title: O - Open/Closed -
task.6.summaryItems.1.text: Add a new animal without touching the old code. Instead of another branch in an `if`-chain, you write a new class behind `IAnimal`. The code that already works is left alone, so it keeps working.
task.6.summaryItems.2.title: L - Liskov Substitution -
task.6.summaryItems.2.text: A subtype has to work anywhere its parent does. A `Penguin` under `Bird` broke that - it threw on `Fly()`. Drop the false claim and let both share a small `IMover` each can honestly keep.
task.6.summaryItems.3.title: I - Interface Segregation -
task.6.summaryItems.3.text: Don't make a class carry methods it never uses. Split the fat interface into `IWalker`, `ISwimmer` and `IFlyer`, and the fish only has to swim.
task.6.summaryItems.4.title: D - Dependency Inversion -
task.6.summaryItems.4.text: Ask for an interface and take it from outside instead of building the real thing yourself. Once the `ILog` is handed in, a test can hand in a fake.
task.6.summaryClose: So when someone asks why bother - each habit earns its place the first time the code has to change. You don't scatter interfaces everywhere up front; you reach for the right fix when a real reason to change turns up. That is the judgement the capstone asks for next.
concept.pr-open-closed.def: Code that is open to new behaviour by adding a type, and closed to editing what already works.
concept.pr-liskov-substitution.def: A subtype must be usable anywhere its base is expected, without breaking the caller's assumptions.
concept.pr-interface-segregation.def: Keeping interfaces small and focused, so a type is not forced to implement methods it does not need.
concept.pr-dependency-inversion.def: High-level code depending on an abstraction rather than a concrete detail, so the detail can change freely.
